title: Icarus and Daedalus
subtitle: The flight too close to the sun
subject: mythologie
description: Daedalus builds wings of wax to escape Crete. His son Icarus flies too high, falls, and gives his name to a sea. A myth about measure and excess.

hero.hook: A father invents wings. A son ignores the warning. The sea still carries his name.

blocks.text: **Icarus** and his father **Daedalus** star in one of the best known Greek myths. Beyond the image of a boy dropping into the sea, the story is about ingenuity, limits, and the pull of going too far.
It is the tale of an impossible escape that turns into a lesson about [[Hybris (and excess)]]: try to match the gods and you risk burning.

sections.title: Daedalus, prisoner of his own labyrinth

blocks.text: **Daedalus** was a legendary inventor, the living image of [[Metis]], the cunning intelligence the Greeks admired. Exiled to the court of King **Minos** in Crete, he built the **Labyrinth**, a prison so tangled that nobody ever walked out. It hid the **Minotaur**, a monster born of the forbidden passion of Queen [[Pasiphae]].

blocks.caption: Daedalus, architect of the Cretan Labyrinth

blocks.text: When Minos learned that Daedalus had helped the hero **Theseus** escape with Ariadne's thread, he shut the inventor and his young son **Icarus** inside their own creation. Land and sea were sealed off. Only the sky was left.
The French word **dédale**, meaning a maze, comes from this character: a place where you lose your way, like the Labyrinth he designed.
By watching birds, Daedalus built two pairs of wings out of wood, feathers and **beeswax**. Craft became the way out.

sections.title: Flying too high, or too low

blocks.text: Before takeoff, Daedalus gave Icarus one simple rule: keep to the middle path. Too low, and the damp air would weigh the feathers down. Too high, and the sun would melt the wax. That caution is close to [[Sophia]], the wisdom of knowing your place.

At first all went well. Father and son flew over the islands of the Aegean. Shepherds below thought they were seeing gods. Then Icarus grew drunk on the flight. He climbed, spellbound by the sky. The wax softened. The feathers came loose. He beat bare arms and dropped into the sea.

blocks.caption: The fall of Icarus, a subject for painters since the Renaissance

blocks.text: The myth is a scientific paradox: the higher you climb, the colder it gets. Icarus should have frozen rather than watched his wax melt.

sections.title: Pride, ideal, or a forgotten detail?

blocks.text: The ancients saw a punishment for pride above all: Icarus paid for wanting too much. The Romantics, **Baudelaire** among them, turned him into a hero of the ideal instead: better to die looking at the sun than to live a careful life on the ground.

The painter **Pieter Bruegel the Elder** offered another reading. In his picture the fall is only a detail: the plowman keeps working, and the world does not stop for a hero. The great individual feat becomes almost invisible.
Some versions add that Daedalus read his son's death as a punishment too: long before, out of jealousy, he had killed his nephew **Perdix**, a rival inventor with too much talent.

sections.title: A sea, an island, a lesson

blocks.text: The currents carried the body of Icarus to an island that the hero **Heracles** named [[Ikaria]]. The water around it became the **Icarian Sea**. Daedalus reached Sicily alone and offered his wings to the god **Apollo**, swearing never to fly again.

The myth survives everywhere: in aviation as both dream and risk, in psychology as the “Icarus complex”, the urge to succeed too fast. Daedalus remains the ambiguous inventor, capable of the best (the wings) and of the worst. [[The labyrinth as a symbol]] reminds us that technology can lock us in as easily as it sets us free.
**Daedalus** escaped Crete on wings of wax. **Icarus** ignored the warning, flew too close to the sun, and drowned. Technology frees us, but without measure it kills.
